overview.text: An optical lens is a shaped transparent element that refracts (bends) light as it enters and leaves, steering rays to form images. Lenses matter because this action helps magnifying glasses, cameras, eyeglasses, and the eye collect or redirect light. A converging lens bends parallel rays toward its optical axis so they meet at a real focal point; a diverging lens spreads rays as if they came from a virtual focal point. The distance from the lens to its focal point is its focal length, a key measure of how it handles light. Lens type and object position affect whether an image can be projected or is seen only by looking through the lens.

key_facts.text: Common converging lenses are thicker at the center than at the edges; common diverging lenses are thinner at the center.
A diverging lens’s focal point is virtual: the outgoing rays spread apart but appear to originate from that point when traced backward.
A converging lens can form a real image when the object is farther from the lens than its focal length, or an upright virtual image when the object is closer.
Lens power is the reciprocal of focal length in meters and is measured in diopters (D).
Light paths are reversible: a source placed at a converging lens’s focal point can emerge as a parallel beam.
